Chapter 6: Network Layer

The OSI Layer 3 role, IPv4 and IPv6, routing decisions and routing tables, router anatomy and boot-up, and configuring a Cisco router.

★ Revision kit — Chapter 6: Network Layer

Eight structured sections for revision: overview, definitions, concept explanations, comparisons, important facts, a knowledge check, common misunderstandings and a quick revision read. Everything here is additive — the complete original slides follow below, unchanged, and every fact links back to its source slide.

1Chapter overviewFrom the course PDFs

Chapter 6 explains OSI Layer 3 end to end. It starts with the network layer's four basic processes — addressing, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulation — and the characteristics of IP (connectionless, best effort, media independent), then contrasts IPv4's limitations with IPv6 (address space, packet handling, no NAT, integrated security). Section 6.2 covers routing decisions: host and router routing tables, default gateways, and how to read show ip route entries (codes, administrative distance, metrics, next hops). Section 6.3 tours the router as a computer — RAM, ROM, NVRAM, flash, interfaces, bootset, show version. Section 6.4 configures a router: mode navigation, passwords/banners, LAN interfaces, verification with show ip interface brief and ping, and host default gateways.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the four basic processes of the network layer and its role as OSI Layer 3 (slides 2–6).
  • Explain IPv4's limitations and the improvements IPv6 brings (slides 7–9).
  • Explain host and router forwarding decisions, default gateways and routing-table structures (slides 11–16).
  • Identify router hardware and memory components and what each stores (slides 18–26).
  • Configure and verify router interfaces and host/switch default gateways (slides 28–32).

Most important concepts

  • Four network-layer processes — addressing, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulation.
  • IP characteristics — connectionless, best effort, media independent.
  • Routing tables — connected (C/L) vs learned remote routes (S, R, D, O…).
  • Default gateway — the exit path for traffic beyond the local network.
  • Router memory model — RAM / ROM / NVRAM / flash and their files.
  • IPv4 vs IPv6 — depletion, NAT and header issues vs 2¹²⁸ addresses, simplified header, integrated security.

2Key definitionsFrom the course PDFs

Network layer (Layer 3)

Provides services that allow end devices to exchange data across the network using four basic processes: addressing end devices, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulating. slide 2

Routing

The network-layer process of choosing the path for packets toward their destination network — the core of a router's job. slide 2

Default gateway

The router interface a host sends to when the destination is not on the local network; hosts keep a local routing table (direct connection, local network route, local default route — e.g. ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 s2/0). slide 12

Routing table

The router's list of known destinations: how each network was learned, the destination network, the interface/next hop used to reach it (show ip route). slide 14

C / L entriesconnected / local

C = the destination network is directly connected on a named interface; L = the router's own local interface address (shown as a /32 host route). slide 15

Administrative distance

The trustworthiness of the route source — the first number in brackets, e.g. [90/2170112] → AD 90 (EIGRP). slide 16

Metric

The cost to reach the remote network — the second bracketed number (here 2170112). slide 16

Next hop

The IP address of the next router on the path (via 209.165.200.226) to reach a remote network. slide 16

RAM

Volatile memory holding the running IOS, running configuration file, IP routing and ARP tables, packet buffer. slide 20

ROM

Non-volatile memory holding bootup instructions, basic diagnostic software and a limited IOS. slide 20

NVRAM

Non-volatile storage of the startup configuration file. slide 20

Flash

Non-volatile storage of the IOS and other system files. slide 20

IPv4Internet Protocol version 4

The network-layer protocol the Internet is still largely based on; an IPv4 packet contains the IP header and the payload; 32-bit dotted-decimal addresses (~4 billion). slide 33

IPv6Internet Protocol version 6

Successor protocol with 128-bit addresses — 8 groups of four hex characters separated by colons (2¹²⁸ ≈ 340 undecillion addresses). slide 9

NATNetwork Address Translation

Referenced by the chapter as part of IPv4's 'lack of end-to-end connectivity'; IPv6 eliminates the need for NAT. slide 7

ICMPInternet Control Message Protocol

The protocol behind ping — the chapter's verification traffic ('Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos … Success rate is 100 percent'). slide 30

3Concept explanationsStudy note

The four processes working together slide 2

To move data end-to-end the network layer: (1) addresses end devices with IP addresses, (2) encapsulates the payload into packets with IP headers, (3) routes packets hop by hop toward the destination network, and at the destination (4) de-encapsulates so upper layers see the original data.

Example: A web request from your PC to a server across the Internet exercises all four on every router it crosses.

Reading a remote routing-table entry slide 16

D 10.1.1.0/24 [90/2170112] via 209.165.200.226, 00:00:05, Serial0/0/0 — piece by piece: D = how it was learned (EIGRP); 10.1.1.0/24 = destination network; 90 = administrative distance (trustworthiness); 2170112 = metric (cost); via 209.165.200.226 = next-hop IP; 00:00:05 = time since discovery; Serial0/0/0 = outgoing interface.

Example: If two sources advertise the same network, the lower administrative distance is more trusted and wins.

Connected vs remote entries slide 15

Connected entries come from configuring an interface with an address: C identifies the destination network and its interface; L is the router's own address on that interface (/32). Remote entries are learned via a routing protocol or static configuration and carry next-hop, AD, metric, elapsed time and outgoing interface.

Example: C 192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0 + L 192.168.10.1/32 appear as soon as you configure G0/0 with .1/24 and bring it up.

Router memory — what lives where slide 20

RAM (volatile): running IOS + running config + routing/ARP tables + packet buffer. NVRAM: startup config (loaded at boot). Flash: the IOS image and system files. ROM: bootup instructions, diagnostics, limited IOS. This is why copy running-config startup-config matters: it copies RAM's active config into NVRAM so it survives power-off.

Example: Power cycle → RAM cleared → router boots IOS from flash, loads startup-config from NVRAM.

When a host needs a default gateway slide 31

A host always keeps a local routing table (direct connection, local network route, local default route). Traffic to a device on the same network needs no gateway; traffic to another network must go to the default gateway's interface. The chapter's two diagrams label exactly these cases: 'Default Gateway not needed' vs 'Default Gateway needed'.

Example: PC1 talking to PC2 in 192.168.10.0/24: direct. PC1 reaching 192.168.11.0/24: via R1's .1 interface.

IPv4's three limitations → IPv6's answers slide 8

IPv4 faces address depletion, routing table expansion and lack of end-to-end connectivity (NAT). IPv6 answers with increased address space (4 billion → 340 undecillion), improved packet handling, eliminating the need for NAT, and integrated security; its simplified header adds routing efficiency, simplified extension headers and per-flow processing.

Example: 2¹²⁸ addresses ≈ 'many trillions for every human on the planet' — the chapter's own phrasing.

Technical terms are kept exactly as the course uses them; the plain-language wording and examples are supplementary study notes.

4ComparisonsFrom the course PDFs

IPv4 vs IPv6

AspectIPv4IPv6
Address size32-bit (~4,000,000,000 addresses)128-bit — 8 groups of four hex chars separated by colons; 2¹²⁸ ≈ 340 undecillion
StatusStill the most widely used network-layer protocol; Internet largely based on itSuccessor with vastly increased address space
NATLack of end-to-end connectivity → NAT neededEliminates the need for NAT
Packet handlingStandard header (IP header + payload)Simplified header: better routing efficiency, simplified extension headers, per-flow processing
SecurityNot integrated in the protocol itselfIntegrated security
Address example192.168.10.2 (dotted decimal)DB52:AA12:5478:001A:EE45:AA25:BB12:FF12

IPv4's limitations as listed: address depletion, routing table expansion, lack of end-to-end connectivity (NAT). slide 7 slide 8 slide 9 slide 33

5Important factsFrom the course PDFs

  • Network layer = OSI Layer 3; four processes: addressing, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulation. slide 2
  • IP characteristics: connectionless, best effort delivery, media independent. slide 6
  • Legacy network-layer protocols mentioned: IPX, AppleTalk, CLNS/DECNet — IPv4 and IPv6 are today's protocols. slide 3
  • IPv4 limitations: address depletion, routing-table expansion, lack of end-to-end connectivity (NAT). slide 7
  • IPv6 benefits: increased address space, improved packet handling, no NAT needed, integrated security; 4 billion vs 340 undecillion addresses. slide 8
  • Host local routing table contents: direct connection, local network route, local default route (example: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 s2/0). slide 12
  • show ip route codes: L local, C connected, S static, R RIP, O OSPF, D EIGRP, * candidate default… slide 14
  • Remote-entry fields: learned-by source, destination network, administrative distance (trustworthiness), metric, next-hop IP, elapsed time, outgoing interface. slide 16
  • Memory: RAM = running IOS/config, routing & ARP tables, buffers; NVRAM = startup config; flash = IOS; ROM = bootup instructions, diagnostics, limited IOS. slide 20
  • show version shows IOS version (e.g. 15.2(4)M1), uptime, last reload reason, interfaces, memory sizes and the configuration register. slide 26
  • Basic configuration flow: enable → configure terminal → hostname → enable secret → line console 0 / line vty 0 4 with password + login → service password-encryption → banner motd → copy running-config startup-config. slide 28
  • Interface configuration: interface gigabitethernet 0/0 → ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0 → description → no shutdown (state changes to up). slide 29
  • Verification: show ip interface brief (status/protocol, addresses) and ping — 'Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos … Success rate is 100 percent (5/5)'. slide 30
  • An IPv4 packet = IP header + payload; the IPv6 simplified header offers routing efficiency, simplified extension headers, per-flow processing. slide 33

6Knowledge checkPractice

8 practice questions — a mix of multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer and explanation tasks. Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, and each one explains why it is correct. These are revision questions written for this site from the course content — they are not lecturer instructions or examination questions.

Multiple choiceQ1. Which set lists the four basic processes of the network layer?

  • A. Addressing, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulation
  • B. Encoding, framing, switching, forwarding
  • C. Authentication, authorization, accounting, auditing
  • D. ARP, DNS, DHCP, ICMP
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — Addressing, encapsulation, routing, de-encapsulation

Why: Slide 2 (and the summary) names exactly these four processes for OSI Layer 3.

True or falseQ2. IP is described as connectionless and providing best effort delivery.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Slides 4–5 are titled 'IP – Connectionless' and 'Best Effort Delivery' — characteristics of the IP protocol.

Multiple choiceQ3. In the entry D 10.1.1.0/24 [90/2170112] via 209.165.200.226, what does 90 represent?

  • A. The administrative distance (trustworthiness of the route source)
  • B. The metric to reach the network
  • C. The interface number
  • D. The number of hops
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — administrative distance

Why: Slide 16: the first bracketed number identifies the administrative distance (trustworthiness); the second (2170112) is the metric.

Short answerQ4. Name the three limitations of IPv4 listed in the chapter.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Address depletion; Internet routing-table expansion; lack of end-to-end connectivity (NAT).

Why: Slide 7 'Limitations of IPv4' lists exactly these three.

Short answerQ5. Which memory types hold (a) the running configuration, (b) the startup configuration, and (c) the IOS image?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: (a) RAM, (b) NVRAM, (c) flash.

Why: Slide 20's memory table: RAM = running config (plus IOS/tables/buffers); NVRAM = startup configuration; flash = IOS and other system files.

Multiple choiceQ6. After configuring an interface, which command pair correctly assigns an address and brings the interface up?

  • A. ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0 then no shutdown
  • B. ip address 192.168.10.1/24 then startup
  • C. address 192.168.10.1 then up
  • D. ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0 then reload
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — ip address … then no shutdown

Why: Slide 29 shows exactly this sequence inside interface gigabitethernet 0/0, with '%LINK-5-CHANGED … state to up' messages following no shutdown.

ExplanationQ7. A PC and a switch both sit on 192.168.10.0/24 with the router at .1. When is a default gateway needed, and what is configured on the switch versus the host?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Traffic to another network (e.g. 192.168.11.0/24) needs a default gateway — the host's local table carries a local default route to the router's interface. Traffic within the same network needs none. The host is given the gateway via its IP configuration; a switch that must be managed from other networks also needs a default gateway configured (the chapter shows both cases as separate slides).

Why: Slides 12 and 31–32: hosts maintain a local routing table with a local default route; the diagrams contrast 'Default Gateway not needed' vs 'needed' and there is a dedicated 'Default Gateway on a Switch' slide.

Short answerQ8. Which two verification commands appear in the chapter, and what does each show?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: show ip interface brief — addresses, status and protocol of every interface; ping — ICMP reachability (example: 5/5, 100 percent).

Why: Slide 30 shows both outputs verbatim.

7Common misunderstandingsStudy note

A default gateway is always required

Only for traffic leaving the local network. The chapter's diagrams show 'Default Gateway not needed' for same-network communication (slide 31).

<code>C</code> and <code>L</code> are the same

C is the connected destination network (192.168.10.0/24); L is the router's own local address on that interface (192.168.10.1/32) — both appear when you configure the interface (slide 15).

Switches and routers use the same tables

Routers make network-layer forwarding decisions from a routing table (connected + learned routes with next hops and metrics); switches forward on MAC tables (Chapter 5) and depend on routers between subnetworks.

Best effort = no design behind delivery

The chapter presents connectionless, best-effort, media-independent IP as characteristics of the protocol (slides 4–6); reliability functions live in upper layers (see Chapter 7), while IPv6 still improves packet handling with its simplified header (slide 33).

8Quick revision (2–5 minutes)Study note

  • Layer 3 four processes: address end devices → encapsulate into packets → route → de-encapsulate. IP = connectionless, best effort, media independent.
  • IPv4 limits: address depletion, routing-table growth, NAT/end-to-end problems. IPv6 answers: 128-bit (8 colon groups; 340 undecillion), improved packet handling, no NAT, integrated security; simplified header → routing efficiency, extension headers, per-flow processing.
  • Host tables: direct connection, local network route, local default route — gateway needed only off-subnet.
  • Reading show ip route: code (C/L/S/R/D/O, * = candidate default) + destination + [AD/metric] + via (next hop) + time + outgoing interface; C = connected network, L = own local address.
  • Router anatomy: it's a computer — RAM (running IOS/config, routing & ARP tables, buffers), NVRAM (startup config), flash (IOS), ROM (boot/diagnostics); show version reports versions, memory, interfaces, config register.
  • Configure: enable → conf t → hostname → enable secret → line console/vty passwords → service password-encryption → banner motd → save (copy running-config startup-config); interface: ip address + description + no shutdown; verify with show ip interface brief and ping.

Identified source-material gaps

Private vs public IP addresses (a comparison you may expect here) is not covered anywhere in this chapter's source material — and a full-corpus search finds no slide that contrasts them — so no comparison is presented rather than fabricating one. RFC 1918 private addressing would need additional source material.
The host and router forwarding-decision slides (11, 13), bootset/boot-up (25), LAN/WAN interface details (23–24), default gateway on a switch (32) and part of the router-configuration walkthrough are figure/output-based — the text above quotes only commands and outputs actually present in the extraction.
IP connectionless/best-effort/media-independent characteristics are named by slide titles (4–6) without further body text — deep behaviour is not expanded in this deck's extractable text.

6.1 Network Layer in Communication

Slide 2
Network Layer in Communication

The Network Layer

The network layer, or OSI Layer 3, provides services to allow end devices to

exchange data across the network. To accomplish this end-to-end transport,

the network layer uses four basic processes:

  • Addressing end devices
  • Encapsulation
  • Routing
  • De-encapsulating

Chapter 6 Summary

1 slide
Slide 33
Network Layer

Summary

In this chapter, you learned:

  • The network layer, or OSI Layer 3, provides services to allow end devices to exchange data across the network.
  • The network layer uses four basic processes: IP addressing for end devices, encapsulation, routing, and de-encapsulation.
  • The Internet is largely based on IPv4, which is still the most widely-used network layer protocol.
  • An IPv4 packet contains the IP header and the payload.
  • The IPv6 simplified header offers several advantages over IPv4, including better routing efficiency, simplified extension headers, and capability for per-flow processing.
